Magnetism.question: At the exact geometric center of a flat circular current-carrying coil, the magnetic field lines are:

options.A: Straight and perpendicular to the plane of the coil
options.B: Concentric circles parallel to the coil plane
options.C: Zero in magnitude

Magnetism.explanation: At the center of a circular current loop, the magnetic field contributions from all wire segments combine into straight, parallel field lines perpendicular to the loop’s plane.

Magnetism.subject: Physics
Magnetism.question: The critical temperature above which a ferromagnetic substance loses its permanent ferromagnetism and behaves as a paramagnetic material is called the:

options.A: Curie Temperature
options.B: Absolute Zero
options.C: Inversion Temperature

Magnetism.explanation: At the Curie temperature, thermal kinetic agitation destroys the alignment of magnetic domains in ferromagnetic substances (e.g., $770^\circ\text{C}$ for iron).

Magnetism.subject: Physics
Magnetism.question: When using the Right-Hand Grip Rule for a solenoid, if the curled fingers point in the direction of conventional electric current, the extended thumb points towards the:

options.A: Magnetic North Pole of the solenoid
options.B: Magnetic South Pole of the solenoid
options.C: Direction of electron flow

Magnetism.explanation: By the Right-Hand Grip Rule for coils and solenoids, the thumb points in the direction of the internal magnetic field, which is toward the magnetic North pole.

Magnetism.subject: Physics
Magnetism.question: The lifting force of an industrial electromagnet used in scrapyards can be effectively increased by:

options.A: Increasing the electric current and the number of turns in the coil
options.B: Decreasing the number of turns of wire
options.C: Replacing the soft iron core with a plastic core

Magnetism.explanation: Magnetic field strength $B \propto n I$. Increasing the number of turns per unit length ($n$) and current ($I$) directly strengthens the electromagnet.

Magnetism.subject: Physics
Magnetism.question: Materials like copper, bismuth, and water that are feebly repelled by strong magnetic fields are classified as:

options.A: Diamagnetic materials
options.B: Paramagnetic materials
options.C: Ferromagnetic materials

Magnetism.explanation: Diamagnetic substances are weakly repelled by magnets because an applied magnetic field induces a weak opposing magnetic moment in their atomic orbitals.

Magnetism.subject: Physics
Magnetism.question: Hans Christian Oersted experimentally discovered that an electric current creates a magnetic field when he observed that:

options.A: A nearby magnetic compass needle deflected whenever an electric current passed through a nearby wire
options.B: An electric charge was created on a dry glass rod
options.C: A bar magnet fell faster through an empty glass tube
options.D: Iron filings melted when touched with a wire

Magnetism.explanation: In 1820, Oersted discovered electromagnetism by noticing that a current-carrying wire deflected a nearby magnetic compass needle, proving that electric currents produce surrounding magnetic fields.

Magnetism.subject: Physics
Magnetism.question: The angle of dip (or magnetic inclination) made by the Earth’s total magnetic field vector with the horizontal plane at the Earth’s magnetic equator is:

options.A: $0^\circ$
options.B: $90^\circ$
options.C: $45^\circ$

Magnetism.explanation: At the Earth's magnetic equator, the Earth’s magnetic field lines are parallel to the horizontal surface, so the angle of dip is $0^\circ$. At the magnetic poles, the field lines are vertical (dip $= 90^\circ$).

Magnetism.subject: Physics
Magnetism.question: A permanent bar magnet can be demagnetized effectively using an electrical method by:

options.A: Placing it inside a solenoid connected to an alternating current (AC) source oriented East-West and slowly withdrawing it
options.B: Connecting both ends of the magnet directly to a direct current (DC) battery
options.C: Submerging the magnet in ice-cold salt water
options.D: Wrapping the magnet in plastic insulation

Magnetism.explanation: Alternating current (AC) reverses magnetic field direction rapidly. Slowly withdrawing the magnet while the AC field decays leaves the magnetic domains randomly oriented, resulting in complete demagnetization.

Magnetism.subject: Physics
Magnetism.question: In the magnetic field mapping around a permanent bar magnet placed on a table, "Neutral Points" are specific points where:

options.A: The magnetic field of the bar magnet is equal in magnitude and opposite in direction to the Earth’s horizontal magnetic field, resulting in a net magnetic field of zero
options.B: The magnetic field strength reaches its absolute maximum value
options.C: A compass needle spins continuously at high speed
options.D: Magnetic field lines cross and intersect each other

Magnetism.explanation: Neutral points are locations where the magnet’s magnetic field exactly cancels out the Earth’s horizontal magnetic field ($B_{\text{magnet}} = B_{\text{Earth}}$ in opposite directions), so the net magnetic field is zero.

Magnetism.subject: Physics
Magnetism.question: When the North pole of a permanent bar magnet is brought close to (without touching) one end of an unmagnetized soft iron bar, the nearer end of the iron bar acquires an:

options.A: Induced South pole (and is attracted)
options.B: Induced North pole (and is repelled)
options.C: Permanent North pole

Magnetism.explanation: By magnetic induction, magnetic domains in the soft iron align so that an opposite pole (South pole) is induced at the nearer end, creating an attractive magnetic force.

Magnetism.subject: Physics
Magnetism.question: Which of the following alloys is categorized as a "hard magnetic material" suitable for manufacturing strong, long-lasting permanent magnets?

options.A: Alnico (alloy of aluminum, nickel, and cobalt)
options.B: Soft annealed iron
options.C: Pure electrolytic copper

Magnetism.explanation: Alnico, steel, and neodymium alloys are magnetically hard materials with high retentivity and coercivity, retaining strong magnetization permanently.

Magnetism.subject: Physics
Magnetism.question: The pattern of magnetic field lines produced around a long, straight conductor carrying a steady electric current consists of:

options.A: Concentric circles centered on the wire axis in planes perpendicular to the wire
options.B: Straight parallel lines radiating outwards away from the wire
options.C: Helical spirals traveling along the length of the wire
options.D: Elliptical loops parallel to the conductor

Magnetism.explanation: The magnetic field of a straight current-carrying wire forms concentric circular field lines centered on the wire, whose direction is determined by the Right-Hand Grip Rule.

Magnetism.subject: Physics
Magnetism.question: In a magnetic field diagram of a permanent bar magnet, as the distance from the magnetic pole increases, the field lines become wider apart, indicating that:

options.A: The magnetic field strength decreases steadily with increasing distance
options.B: The magnetic field becomes uniform and constant
options.C: The polarity of the magnet reverses spontaneously
options.D: The field lines cross one another

Magnetism.explanation: The density/closeness of magnetic field lines is directly proportional to the magnetic field strength. Closer lines near poles represent strong magnetic field; widening lines indicate weakening field strength.

Magnetism.subject: Physics
Magnetism.question: In an electric bell mechanism, the continuous ringing action when the push-button switch is held down occurs because of the:

options.A: Make-and-break contact screw that repeatedly completes and interrupts the electromagnet circuit
options.B: Permanent magnet that rotates continuously
options.C: Thermal expansion of the copper bell gong
options.D: Continuous chemical reaction inside the striker

Magnetism.explanation: When current energizes the electromagnet, it attracts the armature and strikes the gong; this pulls the spring away from the contact screw, breaking the circuit. The spring returns the armature, re-establishing contact in a rapid make-and-break cycle.

Magnetism.subject: Physics
Magnetism.question: Earth’s Magnetic Declination at any geographical location is defined as the angle between the:

options.A: True geographic meridian (True North) and the magnetic meridian (Magnetic North)
options.B: Horizontal magnetic field and the vertical magnetic field component
options.C: Magnetic equator and the geographic equator
options.D: Earth’s rotational axis and the plane of the Moon’s orbit

Magnetism.explanation: Magnetic Declination (or magnetic variation) is the horizontal angle between true geographic North (geographic meridian) and the direction indicated by a magnetic compass (magnetic meridian).

Magnetism.subject: Physics
Magnetism.question: Which of the following materials is a ferromagnetic substance strongly attracted by magnetic fields?

options.A: Cobalt
options.B: Copper
options.C: Aluminum

Magnetism.explanation: Cobalt, Iron, Nickel, and their alloys are ferromagnetic materials with high magnetic permeability that are strongly attracted by magnets.

Magnetism.subject: Physics
Magnetism.question: Why is soft iron preferred over hard steel for the core of electromagnets and electric bells?

options.A: Soft iron is easily magnetized and rapidly loses its magnetism when the current is switched off
options.B: Soft iron becomes a permanent magnet permanently
options.C: Soft iron has zero electrical conductivity
options.D: Soft iron is much harder than steel

Magnetism.explanation: Soft iron is a temporary magnetic material with high permeability and low retentivity/coercivity, allowing it to magnetize instantly when current flows and demagnetize immediately when current stops.

Magnetism.subject: Physics
Magnetism.question: What is the most effective method for completely demagnetizing a permanent steel bar magnet in the laboratory?

options.A: Placing it inside an East-West aligned solenoid carrying AC current and slowly withdrawing it
options.B: Immersing it in cold ice water
options.C: Stroking it repeatedly in one direction with a copper rod
options.D: Connecting it to a direct current (DC) battery

Magnetism.explanation: Alternating current (AC) rapidly reverses magnetic domain orientation. Slowly withdrawing the magnet from an energized AC solenoid oriented East-West leaves magnetic domains randomized, neutralizing net magnetism.

Magnetism.subject: Physics
Magnetism.question: If a bar magnet is cut into two equal halves transversely through its middle, what is the result?

options.A: Two complete smaller magnets, each possessing both a North and a South pole
options.B: One piece with only a North pole and one piece with only a South pole
options.C: Both pieces become completely unmagnetized
options.D: One piece remains magnetic while the other loses magnetism

Magnetism.explanation: Magnetic monopoles do not exist in nature. Cutting a bar magnet produces new opposite poles at the cut faces, creating two complete bipolar magnets.

Magnetism.subject: Physics
Magnetism.question: In the external region surrounding a permanent bar magnet, magnetic field lines are directed from:

options.A: North pole to South pole
options.B: South pole to North pole
options.C: Center of magnet outwards radially in all directions

Magnetism.explanation: By standard scientific convention, external magnetic field lines emerge from the North pole and curve around to enter the South pole, forming continuous closed loops.

Magnetism.subject: Physics
Magnetism.question: How can sensitive electronic circuits and mechanical watches be effectively shielded from external stray magnetic fields?

options.A: Enclosing them in a soft iron magnetic screening casing
options.B: Wrapping them with thick copper foil
options.C: Surrounding them with permanent bar magnets
options.D: Placing them in an airtight plastic vacuum container

Magnetism.explanation: Soft iron has very high magnetic permeability. Magnetic field lines preferentially pass through the soft iron shield walls rather than entering the hollow interior (magnetic screening).

Magnetism.subject: Physics
Magnetism.question: The strength of the magnetic field produced inside a current-carrying solenoid can be enhanced by:

options.A: Inserting a soft iron core and increasing the electric current
options.B: Decreasing the number of coil turns per unit length
options.C: Replacing the copper coil with an insulator
options.D: Increasing the diameter while keeping coil turns constant

Magnetism.explanation: The solenoid field strength is $B = \mu n I$. It is increased by raising current $I$, increasing turn density $n$, and adding a high-permeability soft iron core.

Magnetism.subject: Physics
Magnetism.question: Which magnetic interaction test is considered the ONLY sure, definitive proof that an unknown metallic specimen is magnetized?

options.A: Magnetic repulsion with a known pole of a magnet
options.B: Magnetic attraction to a known pole of a magnet
options.C: Ability to conduct electric current

Magnetism.explanation: An unmagnetized magnetic material (like soft iron) is attracted by both poles of a magnet. Repulsion occurs only between two like magnetic poles, making repulsion the only sure test of magnetization.

Magnetism.subject: Physics
Magnetism.question: What is the geometric shape of magnetic field lines in the plane perpendicular to a long straight current-carrying wire?

options.A: Concentric circles centered on the wire
options.B: Straight parallel lines radiating outwards
options.C: Elliptical loops extending to infinity

Magnetism.explanation: The magnetic field of a straight current-carrying conductor consists of concentric circular lines centered on the wire, whose direction is given by the Right-Hand Grip Rule.

Magnetism.subject: Physics
Magnetism.question: Permanent magnets are manufactured primarily from hard steel or Alnico alloys because these materials possess:

options.A: High magnetic retentivity and high coercivity
options.B: Low magnetic retentivity and zero resistance
options.C: High thermal expansion and low density

Magnetism.explanation: High retentivity ensures strong residual magnetism, while high coercivity resists demagnetization from stray fields, shocks, and temperature variations.

Nature of Science and Physics.subject: Physics
Nature of Science and Physics.question: Ibn al-Haytham (Alhazen) is celebrated as the "Father of Modern Optics" for authoring the monumental treatise:

options.A: *Kitab al-Manazir* (Book of Optics)
options.B: *Al-Qanun fi al-Tibb*
options.C: *Kitab al-Jabr*

Nature of Science and Physics.explanation: Ibn al-Haytham's *Kitab al-Manazir* established the modern ray theory of vision, laws of reflection and refraction, and the pinhole camera (camera obscura).

Nature of Science and Physics.subject: Physics
Nature of Science and Physics.question: Abu Rayhan Al-Biruni determined the radius and circumference of the Earth with remarkable precision at Nandana (Punjab) using:

options.A: Trigonometric dip-angle measurement from the top of a mountain
options.B: Astronomical satellite telemetry
options.C: Measuring the speed of sound in air

Nature of Science and Physics.explanation: Al-Biruni calculated the radius of Earth ($R \approx 6338\text{ km}$) by measuring the angle of dip of the horizon from the summit of a hill using trigonometry.

Nature of Science and Physics.subject: Physics
Nature of Science and Physics.question: Physics is fundamentally defined as the branch of science that deals with the study of:

options.A: Matter, energy, and the mutual interaction between them
options.B: Living organisms and their anatomical structures
options.C: Chemical reactions of organic polymers

Nature of Science and Physics.explanation: Physics is the foundational natural science investigating matter, energy, space, time, and fundamental forces.

Nature of Science and Physics.subject: Physics
Nature of Science and Physics.question: The branch of physics that deals with the study of ionized states of matter containing ions and free electrons at high temperatures is called:

options.A: Plasma Physics
options.B: Solid State Physics
options.C: Nuclear Physics

Nature of Science and Physics.explanation: Plasma is the fourth state of matter consisting of ionized gas, studied in Plasma Physics.

Nature of Science and Physics.subject: Physics
Nature of Science and Physics.question: In the empirical scientific method, a tentative, testable explanation formulated from preliminary observations is called a:

options.A: Hypothesis
options.B: Scientific Law
options.C: Universal Constant

Nature of Science and Physics.explanation: A hypothesis is a proposed, testable explanation formulated prior to experimental verification.

Nature of Science and Physics.subject: Physics
Nature of Science and Physics.question: An error in measurement that occurs consistently in one direction due to faulty calibration or zero error of a measuring instrument is classified as a:

options.A: Systematic error
options.B: Random error
options.C: Human error

Nature of Science and Physics.explanation: Systematic errors arise from known identifiable causes (like instrument zero error) and bias readings consistently.

Nature of Science and Physics.subject: Physics
Nature of Science and Physics.question: The branch of physics concerned with the structure, properties, and reactions occurring inside the atomic nucleus is:

options.A: Nuclear Physics
options.B: Atomic Physics
options.C: Thermodynamics

Nature of Science and Physics.explanation: Nuclear physics specifically studies the atomic nucleus, nuclear forces, radioactivity, fission, and fusion.

Nature of Science and Physics.subject: Physics
Nature of Science and Physics.question: Ibn al-Haytham demonstrated that light travels in straight lines and formed inverted images on a screen using the:

options.A: Pinhole camera (*Al-Bayt al-Muthlim* / Camera Obscura)
options.B: Compound microscope
options.C: Astronomical refracting telescope

Nature of Science and Physics.explanation: Ibn al-Haytham invented the camera obscura (*Al-Bayt al-Muthlim*), demonstrating rectilinear propagation of light.

Nature of Science and Physics.subject: Physics
Nature of Science and Physics.question: While conducting experiments involving high voltage electrical power supplies or laser sources in a physics laboratory, a student MUST:

options.A: Never look directly into the laser beam and ensure circuits are de-energized before making adjustments
options.B: Work with wet hands to increase conductivity
options.C: Bypass safety fuses to increase current

Nature of Science and Physics.explanation: Laser radiation causes permanent retinal damage and high voltage poses lethal shock risk unless strict safety procedures are maintained.

Nature of Science and Physics.subject: Physics
Nature of Science and Physics.question: In physical measurements, the degree of closeness of a measured value to the true/accepted standard value is known as:

options.A: Accuracy
options.B: Precision
options.C: Least count

Nature of Science and Physics.explanation: Accuracy measures closeness to the true standard value, whereas precision refers to the reproducibility and resolution of measurements.

Nature of Science and Physics.subject: Physics
Nature of Science and Physics.question: Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi made groundbreaking contributions to scientific calculation and mathematics through his seminal book:

options.A: *Kitab al-Jabr wa-l-Muqabala* (The Compendious Book on Calculation by Completion and Balancing)
options.B: *Al-Hawi*
options.C: *Canon of Medicine*

Nature of Science and Physics.explanation: Al-Khwarizmi's *Kitab al-Jabr* founded algebra, introduced decimal positional algorithms, and provided mathematical tools fundamental to physics.

Nature of Science and Physics.subject: Physics
Nature of Science and Physics.question: The branch of physics that studies heat and temperature, and their relation to energy, work, and properties of matter is:

options.A: Thermodynamics
options.B: Electrodynamics
options.C: Astrophysics

Nature of Science and Physics.explanation: Thermodynamics is the branch of physics dealing with heat, temperature, thermal processes, heat engines, and energy transformations.

Nature of Science and Physics.subject: Physics
Nature of Science and Physics.question: Pakistani theoretical physicist Professor Dr. Abdus Salam was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics (1979) for:

options.A: The Electroweak Unification Theory unifying electromagnetic and weak nuclear forces
options.B: The invention of the scanning electron microscope
options.C: The discovery of the neutron

Nature of Science and Physics.explanation: Dr. Abdus Salam shared the 1979 Nobel Prize in Physics with Sheldon Glashow and Steven Weinberg for unifying the electromagnetic and weak nuclear forces into the Electroweak Force.

Nature of Science and Physics.subject: Physics
Nature of Science and Physics.question: Random errors in laboratory measurements arise from unpredictable ambient fluctuations or human reading variations. Random error is best minimized by:

options.A: Taking multiple independent readings and calculating their arithmetic average (mean)
options.B: Adding a constant zero correction to every reading
options.C: Using only mechanical spring balances

Nature of Science and Physics.explanation: Because random errors scatter symmetrically above and below the true value, computing the mean of repeated measurements cancels out statistical deviations.

Nature of Science and Physics.subject: Physics
Nature of Science and Physics.question: In physics, a concise verbal statement or mathematical equation describing an established, universal pattern of nature under specified conditions is called a:

options.A: Scientific Law (e.g. Newton's Law of Gravitation, $F = G\frac{m_1 m_2}{r^2}$)
options.B: Hypothesis
options.C: Speculation

Nature of Science and Physics.explanation: A scientific law summarizes an observed regular phenomenon or universal relationship (often mathematically) supported by extensive empirical validation.

Nature of Science and Physics.subject: Physics
Nature of Science and Physics.question: The interdisciplinary branch of science that applies the principles and methods of physics to understand biological phenomena and molecular living systems is:

options.A: Biophysics
options.B: Geophysics
options.C: Astrophysics

Nature of Science and Physics.explanation: Biophysics applies physical principles (optics, thermodynamics, mechanics, electricity) to biological structures such as nerve impulses, DNA, and cell membranes.

Nature of Science and Physics.subject: Physics
Nature of Science and Physics.question: Parallax error in measuring instruments with needle pointers or graduated scales occurs when:

options.A: The observer's eye is positioned at an oblique angle rather than perpendicular to the scale
options.B: The room temperature changes during the experiment
options.C: The scale has an incorrect zero marking

Nature of Science and Physics.explanation: Parallax error is an optical error caused by viewing a scale and pointer from an inclined angle instead of looking perpendicularly directly above the marking.

Nature of Science and Physics.subject: Physics
Nature of Science and Physics.question: Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) scanners utilized in hospital diagnostics rely primarily on principles from which subfields of physics?

options.A: Strong magnetic fields and radiofrequency electromagnetic resonance of hydrogen nuclei
options.B: X-ray ionizing radiation only
options.C: Ultrasound mechanical waves only

Nature of Science and Physics.explanation: MRI utilizes strong superconducting magnetic fields and radiofrequency electromagnetic pulses to image proton spins in body tissues without ionizing radiation.

Nature of Science and Physics.subject: Physics
Nature of Science and Physics.question: The branch of physics that applies physical laws (seismology, magnetism, gravity) to study the interior structure and dynamics of the Earth is called:

options.A: Geophysics
options.B: Astrophysics
options.C: Plasma Physics

Nature of Science and Physics.explanation: Geophysics investigates Earth's internal core, tectonic plate movements, earthquakes, volcanic activity, and geomagnetic fields.

Nature of Science and Physics.subject: Physics
Nature of Science and Physics.question: In the event of an electrical fire breaking out in a physics laboratory equipment rack, the appropriate fire extinguisher to use is:

options.A: Carbon Dioxide ($\text{CO}_2$) or Dry Powder extinguisher (never water)
options.B: A bucket of tap water
options.C: A stream of oxygen gas
options.D: Covering the rack with a wet towel

Nature of Science and Physics.explanation: Water conducts electricity and presents severe electrocution hazards on live electrical fires. Non-conducting $\text{CO}_2$ or dry chemical powder extinguishers are mandatory.

Nature of Science and Physics.subject: Physics
Nature of Science and Physics.question: The renowned 9th-century Muslim polymath Yaqub ibn Ishaq al-Kindi made foundational scientific contributions to the physics of:

options.A: Geometric optics, acoustics, and the theory of light reflection
options.B: Nuclear fission reactors
options.C: Quantum electrodynamics

Nature of Science and Physics.explanation: Al-Kindi authored seminal treatises on geometric optics, the rectilinear propagation of light, optical reflections from curved mirrors, and musical acoustics.

Nature of Science and Physics.subject: Physics
Nature of Science and Physics.question: The specialized branch of physics that investigates the physical properties, evolution, mechanics, and structure of celestial bodies, stars, and galaxies is:

options.A: Astrophysics
options.B: Geophysics
options.C: Biophysics

Nature of Science and Physics.explanation: Astrophysics applies physical laws to understand celestial objects and phenomena across the cosmos.

Nature of Science and Physics.subject: Physics
Nature of Science and Physics.question: The branch of physics that investigates the physical, crystalline, electrical, and magnetic properties of solid matter is termed:

options.A: Solid State Physics (Condensed Matter Physics)
options.B: Nuclear Physics
options.C: Acoustics

Nature of Science and Physics.explanation: Solid State Physics deals with the structural, electronic, and magnetic properties of crystalline solids, which is essential for semiconductor microchips.

Nature of Science and Physics.subject: Physics
Nature of Science and Physics.question: In the empirical scientific method, a "Scientific Theory" is fundamentally characterized as:

options.A: A comprehensive, experimentally verified explanation of natural phenomena supported by a vast body of empirical evidence
options.B: An unverified wild guess by a researcher
options.C: A single isolated measurement reading
options.D: A mathematical formula that never requires testing

Nature of Science and Physics.explanation: In science, a theory is a rigorous, widely tested, and verified explanatory framework that unifies and explains a broad range of natural phenomena.

Nature of Science and Physics.subject: Physics
Nature of Science and Physics.question: In experimental physical measurements, the term "Precision" specifically describes:

options.A: The closeness of agreement between several repeated measurements of the same quantity under identical conditions
options.B: The agreement between a measured value and the true theoretical standard
options.C: The total cost of the measuring apparatus
options.D: The weight of the measuring scale

Nature of Science and Physics.explanation: Precision refers to repeatability and consistency among repeated measurements, whereas accuracy refers to closeness to the true accepted value.

Nature of Science and Physics.subject: Physics
Nature of Science and Physics.question: An experimental error arising from careless handling, incorrect technique, or biased visual alignment by the human experimenter is classified as a:

options.A: Personal error
options.B: Systematic zero error of the tool
options.C: Unavoidable quantum fluctuation

Nature of Science and Physics.explanation: Personal errors occur due to human mistakes, inexperience, poor parallax alignment, or improper technique by the individual conducting the experiment.

Nature of Science and Physics.subject: Physics
Nature of Science and Physics.question: The branch of physics that studies the production, propagation, properties, and technological reception of sound waves and ultrasound is:

options.A: Acoustics
options.B: Optics
options.C: Thermodynamics

Nature of Science and Physics.explanation: Acoustics is the branch of physics focused on the study of all mechanical waves in gases, liquids, and solids, including vibration, sound, ultrasound, and infrasound.

Nature of Science and Physics.subject: Physics
Nature of Science and Physics.question: When performing experiments in a physics laboratory involving laser beams, what is the most critical personal safety protocol?

options.A: Wear specialized wavelength-filtered protective laser goggles and never look directly into the beam
options.B: Keep the room completely dark without ventilation
options.C: Touch the laser aperture with bare hands
options.D: Place reflective glass mirrors directly in the beam path

Nature of Science and Physics.explanation: Laser radiation can cause permanent retinal burns; certified wavelength-protective eyewear is required and looking directly into the beam is strictly prohibited.

Nature of Science and Physics.subject: Physics
Nature of Science and Physics.question: The fundamental branch of classical physics dedicated to the study of light generation, reflection, refraction, lenses, and optical instruments is:

options.A: Optics
options.B: Electrodynamics
options.C: Thermodynamics

Nature of Science and Physics.explanation: Optics is the branch of physics that studies the behavior and properties of light, including its interactions with matter and the construction of optical instruments.

Nature of Science and Physics.subject: Physics
Nature of Science and Physics.question: The development of Medical Imaging technologies such as X-ray Radiography, CT Scanners, and MRI demonstrate that:

options.A: Fundamental physics discoveries provide the foundational principles for advanced healthcare and diagnostic equipment
options.B: Physics has no relevance to biological sciences
options.C: Modern medicine operates without physical laws
options.D: Diagnostic machines are purely chemical devices

Nature of Science and Physics.explanation: Major diagnostic tools (X-rays, CT scanners, MRI, ultrasound, radiotherapy) were directly born from discoveries in electromagnetism, nuclear physics, and acoustics.

Nature of Science and Physics.subject: Physics
Nature of Science and Physics.question: The renowned 11th-century polymath Ibn al-Haytham revolutionized experimental physics primarily through his masterpiece book entitled:

options.A: Kitab al-Manazir (The Book of Optics)
options.B: Al-Qanun fi al-Tibb (The Canon of Medicine)
options.C: Kitab al-Jabr wa al-Muqabala

Nature of Science and Physics.explanation: Ibn al-Haytham (Alhazen) authored the monumental seven-volume treatise *Kitab al-Manazir* (*Book of Optics*), establishing the intromission theory of light and the modern experimental scientific method.

Nature of Science and Physics.subject: Physics
Nature of Science and Physics.question: Abu Rayhan Al-Biruni accurately measured the radius of the Earth during the 11th century at Nandana Fort using:

options.A: Trigonometric calculations based on the angle of dip of the horizon measured from a mountain top
options.B: Measuring the distance between two cities on camelback
options.C: Shadow measurements in deep water wells at noon

Nature of Science and Physics.explanation: Al-Biruni determined the height of a hill using trigonometric angle measurements from a level plain, then measured the angle of dip of the sea horizon from the summit to calculate Earth’s radius ($R \approx 6335\text{ km}$) with remarkable accuracy.

Nature of Science and Physics.subject: Physics
Nature of Science and Physics.question: In modern scientific inquiry, the formal process by which independent domain experts evaluate the validity, methodology, and ethics of a scientific paper before publication is:

options.A: Peer review
options.B: Random sampling
options.C: Media broadcasting

Nature of Science and Physics.explanation: Peer review is an essential quality control mechanism in science where other qualified scientists in the same field critically scrutinize research findings, experimental procedures, and data analysis prior to journal publication.

Nature of Science and Physics.subject: Physics
Nature of Science and Physics.question: Unlike random measurement errors, systematic laboratory errors (such as zero error or miscalibrated scale) can be eliminated or corrected by:

options.A: Identifying the calibration offset and mathematically applying the appropriate zero correction
options.B: Taking the arithmetic mean of 100 repeated readings with the same faulty instrument
options.C: Increasing the brightness of the laboratory lights
options.D: Repeating the experiment on a different day of the week

Nature of Science and Physics.explanation: Systematic errors shift all readings consistently in one direction. Averaging repeated readings cannot remove a systematic error; it can only be eliminated by calibrating the apparatus or applying a known zero correction.

Nature of Science and Physics.subject: Physics
Nature of Science and Physics.question: Medical ultrasound diagnostic imaging (Sonography) utilizes which branch and principle of physics to create internal soft tissue images without ionizing radiation?

options.A: Acoustics (high-frequency ultrasonic sound wave reflections from tissue boundaries)
options.B: Nuclear physics (radioactive decay gamma rays)
options.C: Thermodynamics (heat transfer through convection)

Nature of Science and Physics.explanation: Ultrasound machines emit high-frequency acoustic waves ($> 20\text{ kHz}$) into the body and detect their reflections from internal organs and tissue interfaces to generate real-time anatomical images safely.

Nature of Science and Physics.subject: Physics
Nature of Science and Physics.question: Plasma physics is the specialized branch of physics that studies:

options.A: The fourth state of matter consisting of high-temperature ionized gas containing free electrons and positive ions
options.B: Liquid blood plasma and biological circulation
options.C: Crystalline structures of solid minerals
options.D: Sound waves traveling through liquid helium

Nature of Science and Physics.explanation: Plasma physics is the branch of physics that investigates the properties and behavior of ionized matter (plasma), which makes up over 99% of visible matter in the universe, including stars and interstellar space.

Nature of Science and Physics.subject: Physics
Nature of Science and Physics.question: Abu Ali Sina (Avicenna) and Abu Rayhan Al-Biruni made pioneer contributions to experimental physics in determining the:

options.A: Precise specific gravities and densities of metals, liquids, and precious gemstones using hydrostatic balance methods
options.B: Speed of radio waves in space
options.C: Splitting of atomic nuclei in nuclear reactors

Nature of Science and Physics.explanation: Al-Biruni and Ibn Sina designed sophisticated hydrostatic conical balances to determine the specific gravities and densities of various metals, precious gems, and liquids with remarkable precision.

Nature of Science and Physics.subject: Physics
Nature of Science and Physics.question: When performing electrical circuit experiments in a physics laboratory, what essential safety precaution must always be observed to prevent electric shocks?

options.A: Ensure hands and work surfaces are completely dry, switch off the power supply before modifying wiring, and verify equipment grounding
options.B: Touch live wires with wet fingers to check voltage
options.C: Keep power supplies running at maximum voltage while disconnecting cables
options.D: Remove all fuses and circuit breakers from the laboratory distribution box

Nature of Science and Physics.explanation: Water significantly reduces human skin resistance, increasing electric shock hazard. Always keep hands dry, switch off circuit power supplies before adjusting components, and ensure proper grounding.

Nature of Science and Physics.subject: Physics
Nature of Science and Physics.question: In the scientific method, a tentative, testable statement formulated to explain an observed natural phenomenon before experimentation is called a:

options.A: Hypothesis
options.B: Scientific Law
options.C: Scientific Theory

Nature of Science and Physics.explanation: A scientific hypothesis is an initial, educated, testable proposal or explanation based on preliminary observations, which is then subjected to rigorous experimental verification.

Nature of Science and Physics.subject: Physics
Nature of Science and Physics.question: Modern fiber optic telecommunication systems transmit high-speed data signals through optical glass fibers utilizing the fundamental optical principle of:

options.A: Total Internal Reflection
options.B: Thermal radiation
options.C: Magnetic shielding

Nature of Science and Physics.explanation: Light pulses traveling down optical fibers strike the core-cladding boundary at angles greater than the critical angle, undergoing continuous Total Internal Reflection with minimal energy loss.

Nature of Science and Physics.subject: Physics
Nature of Science and Physics.question: Which renowned Muslim scientist is celebrated as the "Father of Modern Optics" for introducing rigorous experimental methodology and publishing *Kitab al-Manazir* (Book of Optics)?

options.A: Ibn al-Haytham (Alhazen)
options.B: Al-Biruni
options.C: Ibn Sina (Avicenna)

Nature of Science and Physics.explanation: Ibn al-Haytham (965–1040 CE) revolutionized optics through experiments on light rays, reflection, refraction, and the pinhole camera (*Kitab al-Manazir*).

Nature of Science and Physics.subject: Physics
Nature of Science and Physics.question: Which Muslim scientist authored *Kitab Mizan al-Hikma* (The Book of the Balance of Wisdom), determining the precise specific gravities of various metals and precious gems?

options.A: Al-Khazini
options.B: Jabir ibn Hayyan
options.C: Al-Razi

Nature of Science and Physics.explanation: Abd al-Rahman al-Khazini designed advanced hydrostatic balances to measure densities and specific gravities of liquids and metals with extraordinary accuracy in *Kitab Mizan al-Hikma*.

Nature of Science and Physics.subject: Physics
Nature of Science and Physics.question: How does a systematic error in measurement differ fundamentally from a random error?

options.A: Systematic error consistently shifts readings in one fixed direction due to calibration or zero defects, whereas random error varies unpredictably
options.B: Systematic error cannot be corrected, while random error is always constant
options.C: Random error occurs only with digital instruments, while systematic error occurs only with analogue instruments
options.D: Systematic error is caused purely by environmental temperature swings

Nature of Science and Physics.explanation: Systematic errors arise from known zero errors, incorrect calibration, or consistent bias and affect all readings equally in one direction. Random errors vary unpredictably in sign and magnitude due to minor fluctuating conditions.

Nature of Science and Physics.subject: Physics
Nature of Science and Physics.question: Which Muslim scholar and physician formulated the precursor concept of momentum (*mayl* or inclination) in his physical treatises?

options.A: Ibn Sina (Avicenna)
options.B: Jabir ibn Hayyan
options.C: Al-Farabi

Nature of Science and Physics.explanation: Ibn Sina proposed that a projectile in motion receives an impetus (*mayl*) that keeps it moving until air resistance exhausts it, anticipating the modern concepts of inertia and momentum.

Nature of Science and Physics.subject: Physics
Nature of Science and Physics.question: In the scientific method, what is the role and definition of a "hypothesis"?

options.A: A tentative, testable proposed explanation for an observed physical phenomenon
options.B: An absolute, unchangeable scientific law verified for centuries
options.C: A mathematical calculation devoid of physical observations
options.D: A subjective philosophical belief that cannot be tested experimentally

Nature of Science and Physics.explanation: A hypothesis is a provisional, testable proposition formulated to explain observations, which can be supported or refuted through controlled experimental verification.

Nature of Science and Physics.subject: Physics
Nature of Science and Physics.question: Which branch of physics is devoted to the study of the production, properties, and confinement of ionized gases (the fourth state of matter)?

options.A: Plasma Physics
options.B: Solid State Physics
options.C: Geophysics

Nature of Science and Physics.explanation: Plasma Physics investigates the ionic state of matter consisting of free electrons and positive ions at extremely high temperatures, which constitutes stars, lightning, and fusion devices.

Nature of Science and Physics.subject: Physics
Nature of Science and Physics.question: Parallax error during physical measurements with an analogue ruler or meter rule is avoided by:

options.A: Positioning the line of sight strictly perpendicular to the scale at the measurement mark
options.B: Looking at the scale from a $45^\circ$ oblique angle
options.C: Using a magnifying glass while viewing from the left side
options.D: Averaging readings taken from extreme diagonal angles

Nature of Science and Physics.explanation: Parallax error occurs when the eye is positioned obliquely relative to the pointer or scale mark. Keeping the eye perpendicularly above the scale line eliminates this optical displacement error.

Nature of Science and Physics.subject: Physics
Nature of Science and Physics.question: In scientific epistemology, how is a scientific law distinguished from a scientific theory?

options.A: A law describes an observed regularity or relationship (often mathematically), while a theory provides a comprehensive explanatory framework for why it happens
options.B: A law is a temporary guess, while a theory is permanent fact
options.C: A theory can be expressed as a mathematical formula, but a law cannot
options.D: Laws apply only to astronomy, whereas theories apply to biology

Nature of Science and Physics.explanation: A scientific law summarizes what happens under specified conditions (e.g. $F = ma$). A scientific theory explains why and how things occur based on extensive empirical evidence (e.g. Kinetic Molecular Theory).

Nature of Science and Physics.subject: Physics
Nature of Science and Physics.question: The operational physics of modern silicon semiconductors, integrated microchips, and photovoltaic solar panels is grounded in:

options.A: Solid State Physics
options.B: Classical Fluid Mechanics
options.C: Astrophysics

Nature of Science and Physics.explanation: Solid State Physics (Condensed Matter Physics) studies the quantum electronic, crystalline, and band structures of solids, providing the foundation for semiconductor diodes, transistors, microprocessors, and solar cells.

Nature of Science and Physics.subject: Physics
Nature of Science and Physics.question: What is the mandatory primary laboratory safety measure when assembling or modifying an electrical experiment circuit?

options.A: Ensure the main power supply is turned off and disconnected before touching circuit components
options.B: Moisten hands with water to increase contact grip
options.C: Use bare uninsulated copper wires without fuse protection
options.D: Increase circuit voltage to maximum before testing

Nature of Science and Physics.explanation: To prevent dangerous electrical shocks, accidental short-circuits, and component burnout, electrical power sources must always be switched off and isolated before making or changing circuit connections.

Dynamics – I.subject: Physics
Dynamics – I.question: Newton’s First Law of Motion is alternatively referred to as the:

options.A: Law of Inertia
options.B: Law of Conservation of Momentum
options.C: Law of Gravitation

Dynamics – I.explanation: Because Newton’s First Law describes the inherent property of matter to resist any change in its state of rest or uniform motion, it is known as the Law of Inertia.

Dynamics – I.subject: Physics
Dynamics – I.question: According to Newton’s Third Law of Motion, action and reaction forces do NOT cancel each other out because they:

options.A: Act on two different interacting bodies
options.B: Act along different angles
options.C: Have unequal magnitudes
options.D: Act at different moments in time

Dynamics – I.explanation: Action and reaction are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, but they act on two different interacting bodies simultaneously, so they never produce equilibrium on a single body.

Dynamics – I.subject: Physics
Dynamics – I.question: A person of mass $60\text{ kg}$ stands on a spring balance inside an elevator that is accelerating upwards at $2\text{ m/s}^2$ ($g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$). The apparent weight registered by the scale is:
Dynamics – I.explanation: For an upward accelerating elevator: Apparent Weight $R = m(g + a) = 60(10 + 2) = 60 \times 12 = 720\text{ N}$.

Dynamics – I.subject: Physics
Dynamics – I.question: If the elevator carrying the $60\text{ kg}$ person accelerates downwards at $3\text{ m/s}^2$ ($g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$), what is the apparent weight reading?
Dynamics – I.explanation: For a downward accelerating elevator: Apparent Weight $R = m(g - a) = 60(10 - 3) = 60 \times 7 = 420\text{ N}$.

Dynamics – I.subject: Physics
Dynamics – I.question: In an Atwood machine, two masses $m_1 = 6\text{ kg}$ and $m_2 = 4\text{ kg}$ hang vertically over a frictionless pulley ($g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$). What is the tension ($T$) in the connecting string?

options.A: $48\text{ N}$
options.B: $24\text{ N}$
options.C: $50\text{ N}$

Dynamics – I.explanation: Tension in Atwood machine when both move vertically: $T = \frac{2m_1 m_2}{m_1 + m_2}g = \frac{2(6)(4)}{6 + 4}(10) = \frac{48}{10} \times 10 = 48\text{ N}$.

Dynamics – I.subject: Physics
Dynamics – I.question: When a horse pulls a heavy cart along a level road, the forward reaction force that propels the entire horse-cart system forward is exerted by:

options.A: The ground pushing forward on the horse's hooves
options.B: The cart pulling back on the horse
options.C: The horse pulling on the cart reins
options.D: The weight of the horse pushing into the ground

Dynamics – I.explanation: By Newton's Third Law, the horse pushes backward on the ground; in reaction, the ground exerts an equal and opposite forward force on the horse's hooves, moving the system forward.

Dynamics – I.subject: Physics
Dynamics – I.question: A body has a mass of $10\text{ kg}$. If its weight on the surface of Jupiter is measured to be $250\text{ N}$, what is the gravitational acceleration ($g$) on Jupiter?

options.B: $2500\text{ N/kg}$
options.C: $2.5\text{ N/kg}$

Dynamics – I.explanation: Since $W = mg$, gravitational acceleration $g = \frac{W}{m} = \frac{250\text{ N}}{10\text{ kg}} = 25\text{ N/kg} = 25\text{ m/s}^2$.

Dynamics – I.subject: Physics
Dynamics – I.question: When a dusty carpet is vigorously beaten with a stick, dust particles separate and fall off primarily due to:

options.A: Inertia of rest of the dust particles
options.B: Gravitational repulsion
options.C: Inertia of motion of the dust particles
options.D: Centripetal forces acting on the carpet

Dynamics – I.explanation: When the carpet is struck, the carpet fibers move suddenly, but the dust particles tend to remain at rest due to inertia of rest, causing them to detach.

Dynamics – I.subject: Physics
Dynamics – I.question: When a car cruises along a straight horizontal highway at a constant velocity of $80\text{ km/h}$, the resultant net unbalanced force acting on the car is:

options.A: $0\text{ N}$
options.B: $80\text{ N}$
options.C: Equal to the driving force of the engine
options.D: Equal to the weight of the car

Dynamics – I.explanation: Constant velocity implies zero acceleration ($a = 0$). By Newton’s Second Law ($F_{\text{net}} = ma$), the net resultant force acting on the car is exactly $0\text{ N}$.

Dynamics – I.subject: Physics
Dynamics – I.question: A rifle recoils backward when fired with a significantly smaller velocity than that of the escaping forward bullet because:

options.A: The rifle has a substantially greater mass than the bullet
options.B: The rifle experiences a smaller force than the bullet
options.C: The bullet has zero momentum

Dynamics – I.explanation: Both bullet and rifle experience equal and opposite momentum changes. Because $a = \frac{F}{m}$ and $v = \frac{p}{m}$, the much larger mass of the rifle results in a much smaller recoil velocity.

Dynamics – I.subject: Physics
Dynamics – I.question: According to Newton’s Second Law of Motion ($F = ma$), what net unbalanced force is required to produce an acceleration of $4\text{ m/s}^2$ in a cart of mass $5\text{ kg}$?

options.A: $20\text{ N}$
options.C: $9\text{ N}$

Dynamics – I.explanation: By Newton's Second Law: $F = ma = 5\text{ kg} \times 4\text{ m/s}^2 = 20\text{ N}$.

Dynamics – I.subject: Physics
Dynamics – I.question: A physical body continues in its state of rest or of uniform motion in a straight line unless acted upon by an external net force. This fundamental law is known as:

options.A: Newton’s First Law of Motion (Law of Inertia)
options.B: Newton’s Second Law of Motion
options.C: Newton’s Third Law of Motion

Dynamics – I.explanation: Newton’s First Law of Motion states that an object remains at rest or in uniform straight motion unless compelled to change that state by an external unbalanced force. It is also called the Law of Inertia.

Dynamics – I.subject: Physics
Dynamics – I.question: If the cable supporting an elevator snaps and the cabin falls freely under Earth's gravity ($a = g$), what apparent weight will a passenger of mass $70\text{ kg}$ experience?

options.A: $0\text{ N}$ (state of apparent weightlessness)

Dynamics – I.explanation: In free fall, the downward acceleration of the elevator is $a = g$. The scale reaction / apparent weight is $R = m(g - a) = m(g - g) = 0\text{ N}$, producing a condition of apparent weightlessness.

Dynamics – I.subject: Physics
Dynamics – I.question: Mass of an object is measured using a beam balance, whereas the gravitational weight of an object is measured using a:

options.A: Spring balance
options.B: Graduated cylinder
options.C: Mercury barometer

Dynamics – I.explanation: A spring balance measures the gravitational force (weight) acting on an object based on spring extension ($F = kx$), whereas a physical beam balance compares unknown mass with standard masses independent of local gravity.

Dynamics – I.subject: Physics
Dynamics – I.question: If the net resultant force applied to an object is doubled ($F \rightarrow 2F$) while its mass is halved ($m \rightarrow m/2$), the resulting acceleration will:

options.A: Increase by a factor of $4$ (quadruple)
options.B: Double (factor of $2$)
options.C: Remain unchanged

Dynamics – I.explanation: From Newton's second law, $a = \frac{F}{m}$. When force is $2F$ and mass is $m/2$, $a' = \frac{2F}{m/2} = 4\left(\frac{F}{m}\right) = 4a$.

Dynamics – I.subject: Physics
Dynamics – I.question: The inertia of a physical body (its resistance to changes in its state of rest or uniform motion) depends solely on its:

options.A: Mass
options.B: Volume
options.C: Velocity

Dynamics – I.explanation: Mass is the quantitative measure of a body's inertia. A more massive body requires a greater force to change its state of motion or rest.

Dynamics – I.subject: Physics
Dynamics – I.question: A rocket propels itself forward in space according to Newton’s Third Law of Motion because:

options.A: The high-speed backward expulsion of exhaust gases exerts an equal and opposite forward reaction force on the rocket
options.B: The rocket pushes against atmospheric air particles
options.C: Gravitational attraction pulls the rocket into orbit
options.D: The exhaust gases become lighter than space vacuum

Dynamics – I.explanation: By Newton’s Third Law, when rocket engines exert a backward force expelling hot combustion gases, the escaping gases exert an equal and opposite forward reaction force on the combustion chamber.

Dynamics – I.subject: Physics
Dynamics – I.question: When a stone of mass $12\text{ kg}$ is transported from the surface of Earth to the Moon ($g_{\text{Moon}} = \frac{1}{6}g_{\text{Earth}}$), which of its fundamental physical properties remains completely invariant and unchanged?

options.A: Its mass ($12\text{ kg}$)
options.B: Its gravitational weight ($120\text{ N}$)
options.C: Its surface contact pressure
options.D: Its escape velocity from the surface

Dynamics – I.explanation: Mass is an intrinsic quantitative property of matter representing its inertia and remains strictly constant everywhere ($12\text{ kg}$), whereas weight depends on local gravitational field strength ($W = mg$) and is reduced by six-fold on the Moon.

Dynamics – I.subject: Physics
Dynamics – I.question: When a passenger steps out of a moving bus onto the ground, he tends to fall forward in the direction of motion primarily because:

options.A: His feet come to rest upon touching the ground while his upper body continues moving forward due to inertia
options.B: Gravity pulls him forward
options.C: Friction pushes his entire body forward
options.D: Air drag pulls his shoulders forward

Dynamics – I.explanation: When feet contact the stationary ground, they are brought to rest by friction, but the upper body continues in forward motion due to inertia of motion, causing the passenger to stumble forward.

Dynamics – I.subject: Physics
Dynamics – I.question: A mass $m$ is suspended at rest by a vertical light rope. The tension force ($T$) developed in the rope is:

options.A: Equal in magnitude and opposite in direction to the gravitational weight ($T = mg$)
options.B: Twice the gravitational weight ($T = 2mg$)
options.C: Half the gravitational weight ($T = 0.5mg$)

Dynamics – I.explanation: For a body at rest in equilibrium, net vertical force is zero ($\Sigma F_y = 0 \Rightarrow T - W = 0 \Rightarrow T = W = mg$). Tension balances the gravitational weight.

Dynamics – I.subject: Physics
Dynamics – I.question: Two masses $m_1 = 6\text{ kg}$ and $m_2 = 4\text{ kg}$ hang vertically from the ends of a light inextensible string over a frictionless pulley (Atwood machine). Taking $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$, the acceleration of the system is:

options.A: $2\text{ m/s}^2$
options.B: $1\text{ m/s}^2$
options.C: $5\text{ m/s}^2$

Dynamics – I.subject: Physics
Dynamics – I.question: When a rifle is fired, the backward recoil force experienced by the shooter is an illustration of:

options.A: Newton's Third Law of Motion (Action and Reaction)
options.B: Newton's First Law of Motion (Law of Inertia)
options.C: Law of Universal Gravitation

Dynamics – I.explanation: According to Newton's Third Law, for every action there is an equal and opposite reaction. The expanding gases exert a forward action force on the bullet, and the bullet exerts an equal and opposite reaction force pushing the rifle backward.

Dynamics – I.subject: Physics
Dynamics – I.question: A body of mass $5\text{ kg}$ is suspended at rest by a vertical light string. Taking $g = 9.8\text{ m/s}^2$, the tension in the string is:

options.A: $49\text{ N}$
options.B: $98\text{ N}$

Dynamics – I.explanation: Since the body is at rest in vertical equilibrium (acceleration $a = 0$), the upward tension in the string balances the downward weight of the object: $T = W = mg = 5\text{ kg} \times 9.8\text{ m/s}^2 = 49\text{ N}$.

Dynamics – I.subject: Physics
Dynamics – I.question: Passengers sitting in a moving bus are jolted forward when the driver suddenly applies brakes. This phenomenon is explained by:

options.A: Inertia of motion of the passengers' upper bodies
options.B: Action-reaction pairs of gravitational forces
options.C: Centripetal force from the wheels

Dynamics – I.explanation: When the bus brakes suddenly, the lower part of the passengers' bodies in contact with the seats comes to rest with the bus, while their upper bodies continue moving forward due to inertia of motion (Newton's 1st Law).

Dynamics – I.subject: Physics
Dynamics – I.question: An object weighs $98\text{ N}$ on the surface of Earth ($g = 9.8\text{ m/s}^2$). What is its mass on the Moon where $g = 1.6\text{ m/s}^2$?

options.A: $10\text{ kg}$
options.B: $16\text{ kg}$

Dynamics – I.explanation: Mass is the quantity of matter and remains constant everywhere: $m = \frac{W}{g} = \frac{98\text{ N}}{9.8\text{ m/s}^2} = 10\text{ kg}$.

Dynamics – I.subject: Physics
Dynamics – I.question: What is the net resultant force acting on a $1500\text{ kg}$ helicopter hovering stationary in mid-air at a fixed altitude?

options.A: $0\text{ N}$ (Zero net force)
options.B: $15000\text{ N}$ directed upwards
options.C: $14700\text{ N}$ directed downwards

Dynamics – I.explanation: According to Newton's First Law, since the helicopter is stationary in static equilibrium ($a = 0$), the upward rotor lift exactly balances the downward gravitational weight, resulting in a net unbalanced force of zero ($F_{\text{net}} = 0$).

Dynamics – I.subject: Physics
Dynamics – I.question: A net force of $20\text{ N}$ produces an acceleration of $4\text{ m/s}^2$ in mass $m_1$ and $5\text{ m/s}^2$ in mass $m_2$. If both masses are tied together, what acceleration will the same $20\text{ N}$ force produce?
Dynamics – I.explanation: $m_1 = \frac{F}{a_1} = \frac{20}{4} = 5\text{ kg}$; $m_2 = \frac{F}{a_2} = \frac{20}{5} = 4\text{ kg}$. Combined mass $M = 5 + 4 = 9\text{ kg}$. Acceleration $a = \frac{F}{M} = \frac{20}{9} \approx 2.22\text{ m/s}^2$.

Dynamics – I.subject: Physics
Dynamics – I.question: An elevator of mass $600\text{ kg}$ is ascending vertically upwards at a constant uniform velocity of $4\text{ m/s}$. The net resultant force acting on the elevator is:

options.A: $0\text{ N}$

Dynamics – I.explanation: Since the elevator is moving at constant velocity, its acceleration is zero ($a = 0$). By Newton's Second Law, net resultant force $F_{net} = ma = 0\text{ N}$. (Tension equals weight).

Dynamics – I.subject: Physics
Dynamics – I.question: A mass of $5\text{ kg}$ is suspended at rest from the ceiling by a vertical cord. Taking $g = 9.8\text{ m/s}^2$, what is the tension in the cord?

options.A: $49\text{ N}$
options.B: $5\text{ N}$
options.C: $0\text{ N}$

Dynamics – I.explanation: At static equilibrium, upward tension balances downward gravitational force (weight): $T = mg = 5\text{ kg} \times 9.8\text{ m/s}^2 = 49\text{ N}$.

Dynamics – I.subject: Physics
Dynamics – I.question: What happens to the acceleration of a body when the net unbalanced force acting on it is tripled while its mass remains constant?

options.A: The acceleration is tripled ($a \to 3a$)
options.B: The acceleration is reduced to one-third
options.C: The acceleration increases by a factor of 9

Dynamics – I.explanation: By Newton's Second Law ($F = ma \implies a = \frac{F}{m}$), acceleration is directly proportional to net force ($a \propto F$). When the net force is tripled with constant mass, the acceleration also triples.

Dynamics – II.subject: Physics
Dynamics – II.question: A constant force of $50\text{ N}$ acts on a body for a time interval of $0.2\text{ s}$. The impulse (change in momentum) imparted to the body is:

options.A: $10\text{ N}\cdot\text{s}$ ($10\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m/s}$)
options.B: $250\text{ N}\cdot\text{s}$
options.C: $50.2\text{ N}\cdot\text{s}$

Dynamics – II.explanation: Impulse $I = \Delta p = F \times \Delta t = 50\text{ N} \times 0.2\text{ s} = 10\text{ N}\cdot\text{s} = 10\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m/s}$.

Dynamics – II.subject: Physics
Dynamics – II.question: In an isolated physical system consisting of two interacting bodies, the total linear momentum is strictly conserved provided that:

options.A: No external unbalanced force acts on the system
options.B: Both bodies travel at supersonic speeds
options.C: Mechanical friction is infinitely large
options.D: The masses of both colliding bodies are strictly identical

Dynamics – II.explanation: The Law of Conservation of Momentum explicitly states that the total linear momentum of an isolated system remains constant provided no external net force acts upon it.

Dynamics – II.subject: Physics
Dynamics – II.question: The centripetal acceleration ($a_c$) of an object moving with uniform linear speed $v$ in a circle of radius $r$ is given by:

options.A: $a_c = \frac{v^2}{r}$
options.B: $a_c = \frac{v}{r^2}$
options.C: $a_c = v^2 r$

Dynamics – II.explanation: Centripetal acceleration is directed toward the center of the circular path and is mathematically given by $a_c = \frac{v^2}{r}$.

Dynamics – II.subject: Physics
Dynamics – II.question: When an airplane banks into a coordinated turn during flight, the necessary centripetal force for the circular path is provided by the:

options.A: Horizontal component of the wings' aerodynamic lift force
options.B: Vertical gravitational weight of the aircraft fuselage
options.C: Rear propulsion thrust from the jet engines
options.D: Downward drag produced by the tail rudder

Dynamics – II.explanation: When an aircraft banks at an angle $\theta$, the aerodynamic lift force tilts, and its horizontal component ($L\sin\theta$) supplies the centripetal force required to execute the turn.

Dynamics – II.subject: Physics
Dynamics – II.question: For any two contacting surfaces, the coefficient of kinetic friction ($\mu_k$) is generally:

options.A: Less than the coefficient of static friction ($\mu_s$)
options.B: Greater than the coefficient of static friction ($\mu_s$)
options.C: Equal to the coefficient of static friction ($\mu_s$)

Dynamics – II.explanation: Once relative motion begins, the microscopic surface irregularities do not interlock as deeply, so $\mu_k < \mu_s$.

Dynamics – II.subject: Physics
Dynamics – II.question: Why are the outer edges of curved railway tracks or expressway curves banked (tilted at an incline angle)?

options.A: To provide the necessary centripetal force through the normal reaction component and prevent derailment or skidding
options.B: To reduce the total gravitational weight of the moving vehicle
options.C: To increase the air resistance acting on the vehicles
options.D: To allow rainwater drainage into the inner ditch only

Dynamics – II.explanation: Banking curves creates a horizontal component of the normal contact reaction force ($N\sin\theta$) that supplies centripetal force without relying solely on friction.

Dynamics – II.subject: Physics
Dynamics – II.question: In the spin dryer of a washing machine, water is spun out of wet clothes through wall perforations because:

options.A: The adhesion force is insufficient to provide the necessary centripetal force to keep droplets in a circular path
options.B: The centrifugal force pushes the clothes inward
options.C: Gravity pulls water droplets radially outwards
options.D: Air pressure inside the drum drops to zero

Dynamics – II.explanation: At high rotational speeds, the adhesive force holding water to clothes cannot provide the large centripetal force required to maintain circular motion, so water flies off tangentially through holes.

Dynamics – II.subject: Physics
Dynamics – II.question: Which of the following mechanical methods is widely employed in machinery to substitute high sliding friction with much lower rolling friction?

options.A: Installing ball bearings or roller bearings between rotating axles
options.B: Roughening the metal contact faces with coarse sandpaper
options.C: Applying chalk powder to the metal bearings
options.D: Tightening the clamp bolts to increase normal pressure

Dynamics – II.explanation: Ball bearings and roller bearings convert sliding friction into rolling friction, significantly reducing frictional energy dissipation and wear in rotating machine parts.

Dynamics – II.subject: Physics
Dynamics – II.question: If two identical balls of equal mass $m$ travel toward each other along a straight line with identical speeds $v$, the total linear momentum of the two-ball system is:

options.A: $0\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m/s}$
options.B: $2mv$
options.C: $mv$

Dynamics – II.explanation: Momentum is a vector quantity: $\vec{p}_{\text{total}} = m v + m(-v) = 0\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m/s}$.

Dynamics – II.subject: Physics
Dynamics – II.question: High-speed trains, sports cars, and airplanes are designed with tapered "streamlined" shapes primarily to:

options.A: Minimize aerodynamic air resistance (fluid friction)
options.B: Increase the normal contact force with the ground
options.C: Prevent the engine from overheating
options.D: Increase rolling friction between wheels and track

Dynamics – II.explanation: Streamlining reduces turbulent airflow and eddy formation, thereby minimizing aerodynamic drag and fluid friction against the moving vehicle.

Dynamics – II.subject: Physics
Dynamics – II.question: Why are the outer tracks of railways and sharp curves of modern high-speed highways banked (elevated):

options.A: To provide a component of the normal reaction force towards the center, supplying the necessary centripetal force
options.B: To decrease the mass of the turning vehicles
options.C: To increase rolling friction to maximum

Dynamics – II.explanation: Banking of roads tilts the normal reaction force so that its horizontal component ($R\sin\theta$) provides the required centripetal force ($F_c = \frac{mv^2}{r}$), preventing vehicles from skidding without relying exclusively on tire friction.

Dynamics – II.subject: Physics
Dynamics – II.question: An athlete of mass $70\text{ kg}$ sprints along a straight track at a velocity of $8\text{ m/s}$. What is the magnitude of the athlete’s linear momentum?

options.A: $560\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m/s}$ (or $560\text{ N}\cdot\text{s}$)
options.B: $280\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m/s}$
options.C: $78\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m/s}$

Dynamics – II.explanation: Momentum $p = mv = 70\text{ kg} \times 8\text{ m/s} = 560\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m/s} = 560\text{ N}\cdot\text{s}$.

Dynamics – II.subject: Physics
Dynamics – II.question: In SI units, the coefficient of friction ($\mu = F_s / R$) between two solid surfaces is expressed in:

options.A: No units (it is a dimensionless ratio)
options.B: Newtons ($\text{N}$)
options.C: $\text{N/m}$

Dynamics – II.explanation: The coefficient of friction is the ratio of limiting frictional force to the normal reaction force ($\mu = F_s / R$). Since it is a ratio of two forces, it has no units and is dimensionless.

Dynamics – II.subject: Physics
Dynamics – II.question: A cricket fielder pulls his hands backward while catching a fast-moving ball in order to:

options.A: Increase the collision time interval, thereby decreasing the impact force exerted on his hands
options.B: Increase the momentum of the ball
options.C: Decrease the total time of the catch
options.D: Increase the reaction force on the ball

Dynamics – II.explanation: From $F = \frac{\Delta p}{\Delta t}$, increasing the time interval $\Delta t$ during which the ball is brought to rest decreases the rate of change of momentum, significantly reducing the impact force on the hands.

Dynamics – II.subject: Physics
Dynamics – II.question: In a medical laboratory centrifuge or cream separator, denser components separate to the outer perimeter of the spinning bowl because:

options.A: Denser particles have greater inertia and require a larger centripetal force than the surrounding fluid can provide
options.B: Denser particles have zero mass in circular motion
options.C: The centrifuge eliminates Earth's gravity
options.D: Lighter particles experience greater gravitational pull

Dynamics – II.explanation: Denser particles have greater mass, thus requiring a larger centripetal force ($F_c = \frac{mv^2}{r}$). Because the fluid cannot supply this force, they move outward to the bottom and perimeter of the spinning tubes.

Dynamics – II.subject: Physics
Dynamics – II.question: The physical quantity defined as the product of an applied force ($F$) and the brief time duration ($\Delta t$) for which it acts ($J = F \times \Delta t$) is the:

options.A: Impulse of the force
options.B: Inertia
options.C: Centripetal acceleration

Dynamics – II.explanation: Impulse is defined as $J = F \times \Delta t$. By the impulse-momentum theorem, impulse equals the total change in linear momentum ($\Delta p$) produced in the body.

Dynamics – II.subject: Physics
Dynamics – II.question: The relationship connecting the kinetic energy ($E_k$) of a moving body of mass $m$ with its linear momentum ($p$) is:

options.A: $E_k = \frac{p^2}{2m}$
options.B: $E_k = \frac{2m}{p^2}$
options.C: $E_k = \frac{p}{2m}$

Dynamics – II.explanation: Since $p = mv \Rightarrow v = \frac{p}{m}$, substituting into kinetic energy gives $E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 = \frac{1}{2}m\left(\frac{p}{m}\right)^2 = \frac{p^2}{2m}$.

Dynamics – II.subject: Physics
Dynamics – II.question: When a car navigates a level, unbanked curved road, what physical force supplies the necessary centripetal force to keep it in the turn?

options.A: Static friction between the car tires and the road surface
options.B: The forward driving force of the engine
options.C: The aerodynamic downward lift of the chassis
options.D: The gravitational weight of the vehicle

Dynamics – II.explanation: On a flat, horizontal circular curve, the centripetal force ($F_c = \frac{mv^2}{r}$) is supplied entirely by the lateral static friction force between the road surface and the tires.

Dynamics – II.subject: Physics
Dynamics – II.question: A bullet of mass $0.02\text{ kg}$ is fired horizontally at $300\text{ m/s}$ from a rifle of mass $3\text{ kg}$. What is the recoil velocity of the rifle?

options.A: $-2\text{ m/s}$ ($2\text{ m/s}$ in the backward direction)
options.B: $-6\text{ m/s}$

Dynamics – II.explanation: By the Law of Conservation of Momentum: $m_b v_b + m_g v_g = 0 \Rightarrow (0.02)(300) + (3)v_g = 0 \Rightarrow 6 + 3v_g = 0 \Rightarrow v_g = -\frac{6}{3} = -2\text{ m/s}$.

Dynamics – II.subject: Physics
Dynamics – II.question: Rolling friction is significantly smaller than sliding friction primarily because:

options.A: The microscopic contact points between a rolling wheel and the surface experience negligible sliding or abrasive rubbing
options.B: Rolling objects experience zero gravitational pull
options.C: The normal reaction force vanishes during rolling
options.D: The coefficient of rolling friction is always negative

Dynamics – II.explanation: In rolling motion, contact with the ground occurs instantaneously along a small contact patch without relative sliding, so microscopic surface interlocks do not rupture abrasively.

Dynamics – II.subject: Physics
Dynamics – II.question: A rifle of mass $4\text{ kg}$ fires a bullet of mass $0.02\text{ kg}$ ($20\text{ g}$) with a muzzle velocity of $400\text{ m/s}$. The recoil velocity of the rifle is:
Dynamics – II.explanation: By law of conservation of momentum: $M_r v_r + m_b v_b = 0 \implies v_r = -\frac{m_b v_b}{M_r} = -\frac{0.02 \times 400}{4} = -2.0\text{ m/s}$ (negative sign indicates recoil in the opposite direction).

Dynamics – II.subject: Physics
Dynamics – II.question: A horizontal pulling force of $30\text{ N}$ is just sufficient to initiate sliding of a $100\text{ N}$ wooden block across a level floor. The coefficient of static friction $\mu_s$ is:
Dynamics – II.explanation: $\mu_s = \frac{F_s}{R} = \frac{30\text{ N}}{100\text{ N}} = 0.30$.

Dynamics – II.subject: Physics
Dynamics – II.question: A car of mass $1000\text{ kg}$ navigates a circular track of radius $50\text{ m}$ at a constant speed of $10\text{ m/s}$. What is the centripetal force required to keep it on the curve?

Dynamics – II.subject: Physics
Dynamics – II.question: Why are highway turns and railway curves banked (outer edge built higher than the inner edge)?

options.A: To provide the necessary centripetal force from the horizontal component of normal reaction
options.B: To increase the force of gravity on the vehicle
options.C: To eliminate rolling friction completely
options.D: To reduce the maximum permissible speed of vehicles

Dynamics – II.explanation: Banking tilts the normal reaction force so that its horizontal component ($R\sin\theta$) provides the required centripetal force, preventing dangerous sideways skidding without relying solely on tyre friction.

Dynamics – II.subject: Physics
Dynamics – II.question: In a centrifuge cream separator, why do less dense cream particles separate and collect near the central axis while denser skim milk is forced outwards?

options.A: Denser milk requires larger centripetal force and is thrown outwards, leaving lighter cream at the center
options.B: Cream particles have greater mass and experience stronger centrifugal repulsion
options.C: Friction between cream and the bowl wall is higher
options.D: Cream particles carry negative electric charges

Dynamics – II.explanation: Centripetal force is directly proportional to mass ($F_c = m\omega^2 r$). The denser skim milk needs and experiences larger inward forces, displacing the lighter cream particles toward the axis of rotation.

Dynamics – II.subject: Physics
Dynamics – II.question: On a curved circular road bend, why is the outer edge of the road banked higher than the inner edge?

options.A: To provide a horizontal component of normal reaction that supplies the required centripetal force
options.B: To eliminate the downward gravitational force acting on the car
options.C: To increase the coefficient of kinetic friction between tires and asphalt
options.D: To reduce the rotational inertia of the car wheels

Dynamics – II.explanation: Banking the track at an angle $\theta$ produces an inward horizontal component of the normal reaction force ($R\sin\theta = \frac{mv^2}{r}$), providing the necessary centripetal force and preventing high-speed vehicles from skidding outward.

Dynamics – II.subject: Physics
Dynamics – II.question: Rolling friction is significantly smaller (often 100 to 1000 times less) than sliding friction primarily because:

options.A: The microscopic area of contact is extremely small and there is no relative sliding/rubbing of surfaces
options.B: Rolling objects experience zero normal reaction force
options.C: Gravitational attraction vanishes during rolling motion
options.D: Rolling surfaces are always coated with lubricants

Dynamics – II.explanation: In rolling motion, contact points momentarily touch and lift without sliding over each other, minimizing the inter-locking and shearing of microscopic cold-welded surface irregularities.

Dynamics – II.subject: Physics
Dynamics – II.question: If the linear speed of a body traversing a circle of constant radius $r$ is tripled ($v \to 3v$), its centripetal acceleration increases by a factor of:
Dynamics – II.explanation: Centripetal acceleration is $a_c = \frac{v^2}{r}$. Since $a_c \propto v^2$, tripling the speed ($3^2 = 9$) increases the acceleration by a factor of 9.

Dynamics – II.subject: Physics
Dynamics – II.question: A $2.0\text{ kg}$ trolley moving at $6.0\text{ m/s}$ collides with and couples to a stationary $4.0\text{ kg}$ trolley. What is their common velocity immediately after collision?

options.A: $2.0\text{ m/s}$
options.B: $3.0\text{ m/s}$
options.C: $1.5\text{ m/s}$

Dynamics – II.explanation: By conservation of momentum: $m_1 u_1 + m_2 u_2 = (m_1 + m_2)v \implies 2(6.0) + 4(0) = (2 + 4)v \implies 12 = 6v \implies v = 2.0\text{ m/s}$.

Dynamics – II.subject: Physics
Dynamics – II.question: Ball bearings and roller bearings are incorporated into wheels and machine axles to:

options.A: Convert sliding friction into much lower rolling friction
options.B: Increase the static friction between shafts
options.C: Reduce the total rotational speed of wheels
options.D: Eliminate all mechanical contact with the axle

Dynamics – II.explanation: Ball bearings replace direct sliding contact with rolling spheres, dramatically reducing friction, heat generation, and mechanical wear.

The Science of Biology.subject: Biology
The Science of Biology.question: Which type of scientific reasoning moves from specific observations to a general scientific principle (e.g., 'All examined birds have wings, therefore all birds have wings')?

options.A: Deductive reasoning
options.B: Inductive reasoning
options.C: Theoretical deduction

The Science of Biology.explanation: Inductive reasoning moves from specific observations to broader generalizations, whereas deductive reasoning flows from general principles to specific testable predictions (if-then logic).

The Science of Biology.subject: Biology
The Science of Biology.question: Which landmark book containing comprehensive descriptions of animal behavior, classification, and social hierarchy was authored by the Muslim scientist Jabir ibn Hayyan or Al-Jahiz?

options.A: *Kitab al-Haywan* (Book of Animals) by Al-Jahiz
options.B: *Al-Nabataat* by Jabir ibn Hayyan
options.C: *Al-Qanun fi al-Tibb* by Bu Ali Sina

The Science of Biology.explanation: Al-Jahiz authored *Kitab al-Haywan* (The Book of Animals), describing animal species, habitats, and environmental adaptations centuries before modern evolutionary ecology.

The Science of Biology.subject: Biology
The Science of Biology.question: The specialized branch of biology that deals with the study of ancestral evolutionary relationships, lineage trees, and fossilized ancestral remains of organisms is:

options.A: Histology
options.B: Paleontology
options.C: Morphology

The Science of Biology.explanation: Paleontology is the scientific study of fossils to determine organisms' evolution, prehistoric lineages, and interactions with environmental pasts.

The Science of Biology.subject: Biology
The Science of Biology.question: In a controlled biological experiment investigating the effect of nitrogen fertilizer on wheat yield, the control group must be:

options.A: Treated with excess double doses of fertilizer
options.B: Kept in complete darkness without irrigation
options.C: Grown under identical environmental conditions but without adding the nitrogen fertilizer
options.D: Replaced by an entirely different crop species such as maize

The Science of Biology.explanation: A control group provides a baseline comparison and is maintained under identical conditions except that it does not receive the experimental variable being tested (the nitrogen fertilizer).

The Science of Biology.subject: Biology
The Science of Biology.question: Which of the following represents the correct ascending hierarchical sequence of biological organization?

options.A: Molecule -> Organelle -> Cell -> Tissue -> Organ -> Organ System -> Organism
options.B: Organelle -> Cell -> Organ -> Tissue -> Molecule -> Community
options.C: Cell -> Molecule -> Tissue -> Organism -> Population -> Biosphere
options.D: Tissue -> Organ -> Cell -> Organelle -> Ecosystem -> Species
